Published 30 September 2026 · By Steve English · All major claims linked to source documents

BREXIT · LABOUR · DEMOCRACY

LABOUR ANNOUNCE NEW EU REFERENDUM

In all but name

  • Labour's 2024 manifesto said Britain would stay outside the EU and ruled out a return to the Single Market, Customs Union and freedom of movement.
  • Andy Burnham has now put the long-term relationship back on the table, including the Single Market, Customs Union and full EU membership.
  • The 2016 Leave majority was 1,269,501 votes.
  • Labour previously backed extending national voting rights to all UK residents, regardless of nationality.

PURPOSE / MISSION: To compare Labour's explicit 2024 Brexit commitments with Andy Burnham's new EU options, then examine the unanswered democratic question that follows if the country is asked to establish a new consensus: who would be entitled to take part?

LABOUR'S BIGGEST U-TURN YET

Britain's future outside the European Union was supposed to be settled Labour policy.

At the 2024 General Election, Labour explicitly promised that Britain would “stay outside of the EU”.

“There will be no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement.”

Those weren't vague aspirations. They were explicit manifesto commitments on which Labour sought and received its mandate to govern.

Now, in Labour's biggest U-turn yet, the Government has put every one of those options back on the table — including full membership of the European Union itself.

At the Labour conference, Prime Minister Andy Burnham announced that he would “lay out to the country” the different options for Britain's future relationship with Europe and attempt to “find consensus around one”.

He has since spelled out those choices.

Britain could stay where it is, enter a customs union, return to the Single Market — or, in Burnham's own words, “go all the way”.

And when asked what “go all the way” meant, Burnham confirmed it: full membership of the European Union.

In other words, Labour is now considering the very options it explicitly ruled out when asking the country to elect it — right through to reversing Brexit itself.

Burnham did not become Prime Minister through a General Election fought on any of these proposals. He became Labour leader and Prime Minister after entering Parliament in 2026.

Burnham has acknowledged that any formal change would have to wait until the next General Election.

That matters.

If Labour wants a mandate to overturn the Brexit settlement it explicitly promised to maintain, the next General Election provides a route to seek one — under the normal Parliamentary franchise, without extending voting rights to non-citizen EU residents.

But that isn't all Burnham has announced.

He intends to “lay out to the country” these competing EU options and “find consensus around one”.

How?

Polling? A national consultation? A referendum? Another form of national vote?

Labour hasn't said.

But whatever terminology or mechanism is eventually chosen, the fundamental question Britain voted on in 2016 is being put back before the country: remain outside the European Union, move progressively closer to it — or ultimately rejoin it.

A referendum by any other name is still asking the country to make a choice about its future relationship with the European Union.

And that leads to another rather important question.

BUT WHO GETS TO VOTE THIS TIME?

The 2016 EU referendum was close.

LEAVE17,410,742
REMAIN16,141,241

A winning margin of just:

1,269,501 VOTES

But Britain — and its electorate — has changed since then.

Since the EU referendum was announced, more than 500,000 EU nationals have acquired British citizenship.

Those people are now British citizens, with the voting rights that come with British citizenship.

But when Labour last proposed another Brexit referendum, it wanted to go considerably further.

Its 2019 manifesto promised what Labour called:

“the largest extension of the franchise in generations”

including:

“giving full voting rights to all UK residents”.

Labour conference had also backed:

“equal rights to vote to all UK residents”

regardless of nationality.

And when challenged specifically about EU nationals being allowed to participate in Labour's proposed second Brexit referendum, senior Labour figure Rebecca Long-Bailey defended the principle:

“It's not right to have a system that denies them the vote.”

That wasn't about the EU nationals who had already become British citizens.

They already possessed British voting rights.

Labour was arguing that EU nationals living in Britain who had not become British citizens should also be allowed to participate.

And that is potentially a very large group.

Census figures recorded approximately 4.1 million non-Irish EU citizens living in the UK. Around 322,000 were already dual British-EU nationals, leaving roughly:

3.8 MILLION NON-BRITISH EU CITIZENS

The latest evidence indicates that the EU-national population has subsequently declined, so that Census figure should not be mistaken for a precise 2026 headcount.

But it demonstrates the scale involved.

Labour later abandoned its second-referendum policy. It abandoned rejoining the EU. It ruled out the Single Market and Customs Union.

And its proposal to extend national voting rights to resident EU nationals disappeared alongside that political programme.

Now those policies are back on the table.

The Customs Union.

The Single Market.

And, with Burnham's “go all the way”, even full EU membership.

So if Labour intends to establish a new “national consensus” on those choices, there is a question it cannot avoid answering.

When Labour last wanted another referendum on Britain's relationship with Europe, it argued that EU nationals living here should have a say.

There are already 500,000+ EU nationals who have become British citizens since the referendum process began, while the potential pool of non-British EU residents runs into the millions.

Labour has not announced that those non-citizens will be given a vote this time.

But given Labour's previous policy, the question is unavoidable:

WILL LABOUR LET THEM
VOTE THIS TIME?
